issues.legal_issue: The central government cannot direct individual allotments or revive a closed housing scheme without authority under the governing statutory framework.
material_facts: The housing scheme had been closed, and the applicants had not responded to a public notice offering another opportunity to apply for flats.
After the applicants sought allotment through administrative representations, a central government communication asked the housing authority to consider their cases under an out-of-turn quota.
The applicants had no successful claim before the consumer fora, and the governing framework gave the central government no quota or power to decide individual allotments.
issues.conclusion: The central government lacked jurisdiction to direct the individual allotments or revive the closed scheme, and its direction was invalid.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 41 and 56(2)(r) of the Delhi Development Act, 1957, the central government may issue directions connected with efficient administration and exercise statutory rule-making power, but those provisions do not authorize it to decide individual allotments or revive a particular scheme. Section 21 of the General Clauses Act could not supply a power that the Act did not confer. M.P. Gangadharan v. State of Kerala was held inapplicable.

rule.if: housing_scheme_allotment_appeal and scheme_was_closed and central_authority_directed_individual_allotments and central_authority_lacked_allotment_power

predicates.housing_scheme_allotment_appeal: The proceeding was an appeal concerning the denial of allotments under a housing scheme.
predicates.scheme_was_closed: The housing authority had closed the scheme before the individual allotment direction was issued.
predicates.central_authority_directed_individual_al: The central authority asked the housing authority to allot or consider flats for particular applicants.
predicates.central_authority_lacked_allotment_power: The governing framework did not give the central authority power to decide individual allotments.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns allotments under a closed housing scheme and the central authority directs individual allotments despite lacking power to do so, the direction is invalid.

issues.legal_issue: A public authority cannot create an ad hoc allotment quota outside its declared scheme and allocation policy without lawful authority.
material_facts: The housing scheme brochure prescribed how flats were to be allotted and identified the categories for which reservations were made.
The central government sought to place the applicants in an out-of-turn quota as hard cases, although that category was not authorized for them by the scheme or the stated policy.
The housing authority was a public body subject to the constitutional requirement of equality.
issues.conclusion: The purported decision to create or apply an unauthorized quota was without jurisdiction and a nullity.
issues.legal_principle: A public authority must act within its lawful framework and comply with the standards and procedures by which it has professed to act. Article 14 of the Constitution precludes arbitrary departures from a declared public scheme. The Court relied on Vitarelli v. Seaton, Ramana Dayaram Shetty v. International Airport Authority of India, and Harjit Singh v. State of Punjab.

rule.if: public_scheme_allotment_dispute and scheme_defined_allocation_categories and officials_created_an_extra_quota and public_authority_was_bound_by_equal_treatment

predicates.public_scheme_allotment_dispute: The proceeding concerned the allocation of benefits under a public housing scheme.
predicates.scheme_defined_allocation_categories: The published scheme specified the categories and method governing allocation.
predicates.officials_created_an_extra_quota: Officials sought to allocate benefits through a category not provided for by the scheme or the governing policy.
predicates.public_authority_was_bound_by_equal_trea: The authority making or implementing the allocation was a public body required to treat applicants consistently and fairly.

issues.definition: When officials create an extra quota in a public scheme that already defines allocation categories, the quota decision is void if the authority is bound by equal treatment.

issues.legal_issue: Administrative guidelines that lack statutory force do not, by themselves, create an enforceable legal right to an allotment.
material_facts: The applicants relied on an administrative communication concerning consideration of their cases under an out-of-turn quota.
The communication did not identify a statutory basis for that quota, and the governing scheme did not provide the applicants with that allotment entitlement.
The applicants sought to enforce the communication as a basis for obtaining flats.
issues.conclusion: The communication and administrative guidance did not confer an enforceable right to allotment.
issues.legal_principle: Guidelines are advisory in character and do not, by themselves, confer legal rights; judicial intervention may be warranted where a departure is arbitrary, discriminatory, or defeats a basic public purpose. The Court relied on Narendra Kumar Maheshwari v. Union of India, Maharao Sahib Shri Bhim Singhji v. Union of India, J.R. Raghupathy v. State of A.P., and Uttam Parkash Bansal v. L.I.C. of India. It also distinguished Union of India v. K.P. Joseph, which concerned an executive order within the issuing authority’s jurisdiction.

predicates.public_scheme_allotment_dispute: The proceeding concerned a claim to an allotment under a public scheme.
predicates.claimed_right_rests_on_administrative_gu: The applicants relied on administrative guidance as the basis for their claimed allotment entitlement.
predicates.guidance_lacked_statutory_force: The guidance was not backed by a statutory rule conferring the claimed entitlement.

issues.definition: If an allotment claim under a public scheme rests on guidance without statutory force, that guidance alone creates no enforceable allotment right.

issues.legal_issue: Legitimate expectation and promissory estoppel cannot make an unlawful and unauthorized allotment direction enforceable.
material_facts: The applicants relied on the central government communication as the basis for an expectation that they would receive flats.
The communication proposed an exception to the governing scheme despite lacking lawful authority.
The applicants identified no regular and consistent practice supporting the claimed expectation.
issues.conclusion: The doctrines of legitimate expectation and promissory estoppel could not be used to enforce the purported allotment direction.
issues.legal_principle: Legitimate expectation may arise from a valid representation or a regular, consistent, predictable, and certain practice, but it cannot be founded on an illegal or unauthorized order. Even a legitimate expectation does not invariably entitle a person to the expected benefit. The Court relied on Ram Pravesh Singh v. State of Bihar.

predicates.allotment_claim_relies_on_expected_admin: The applicants claimed an allotment on the basis of a benefit they expected the administration to provide.
predicates.expectation_is_based_on_an_unlawful_dire: The expected benefit arose from an administrative direction made without lawful authority.
predicates.no_established_practice_supports_expecta: The applicants did not rely on a regular and consistent administrative practice supporting the expected benefit.

issues.definition: Where an expected administrative benefit rests on an unlawful direction and no established practice supports it, those doctrines do not make the direction enforceable.

issues.legal_issue: An administrative order can confer an enforceable right only when it is made by an authority with jurisdiction and, where required, in the constitutionally prescribed form.
material_facts: The applicants relied on a communication from a government officer asking the housing authority to take action on their allotment cases.
The communication did not establish that it was an order made in the constitutionally prescribed form.
The central government lacked authority under the governing framework to direct the individual allotments.
issues.conclusion: The communication did not confer an enforceable legal right to allotment.
issues.legal_principle: A government order that is to confer a legal right must conform to Article 166 of the Constitution. Union of India v. K.P. Joseph does not establish that every executive order creates a right; it concerned an order made within the issuing authority’s jurisdiction. The Court relied on J.P. Bansal v. State of Rajasthan and distinguished K.P. Joseph.

predicates.claim_to_enforce_government_communicatio: The applicants sought to enforce a government communication as the source of an entitlement.
predicates.communication_was_not_made_in_required_c: The communication was not shown to have been made in the form required for a government order conferring a right.
predicates.issuing_authority_lacked_jurisdiction: The authority that issued the communication had no power to direct the individual allotment.

issues.definition: When a claimed right rests on a government communication that was not made in the required constitutional form and whose issuer lacked jurisdiction, the communication confers no enforceable right.
